_note: Hand-labeled synthetic FieldChange/MenuChange scenarios for contract_agent.py's decision layer (Good-to-Go's escalate/review classifier). Deliberately scoped to RULE-decided cases only -- no GEMINI_API_KEY needed, fully deterministic, no network dependency. Genuinely ambiguous free-text changes (an event_type reword, a menu description edit) go through llm_client.judge_contract_change() instead of a rule and aren't covered here -- see evaluation/labeled_llm_judgments.json / evaluate_llm_judgment.py for that path, and docs/DESIGN.md's Limitations section for why LLM-judged paths are validated separately. Scaled from an original 8 cases to this larger set specifically to include adversarial/boundary cases (exact threshold values, OCR-style garbled numbers, cosmetic-only reformatting) rather than only the 'obvious' scenario per rule -- every expected_decision here was checked against contract_agent.py's actual threshold math (SIGNIFICANT_QUANTITY_CHANGE = 0.15, strict '>') before being written, not guessed.

cases.why: location is an always-escalate field -- delivery/logistics depend on it directly, regardless of magnitude
event_time is an always-escalate field, same reasoning as location
a one-character room-letter change is still a location change -- always-escalate fields don't have a magnitude threshold

adversarial: a single-letter diff that LOOKS like an OCR typo rather than a real edit -- the rule deliberately never tries to distinguish a typo from a real change for this field, by design, so it still escalates
a full address swap, same rule as the smaller diffs above

adversarial: this almost certainly refers to the SAME physical place, just written out in full -- the rule doesn't attempt that semantic read and escalates anyway, a deliberate false-positive-by-design tradeoff for a field this operationally important
a single AM/PM token flip is a huge real-world change (12-hour shift) hiding behind a tiny text diff -- confirms the always-escalate rule catches this regardless of how small the string edit looks
adversarial: the opposite direction from the AM/PM case -- a genuinely trivial one-minute shift still escalates, since this field has no magnitude threshold at all
adversarial: same actual time, just annotated -- the rule doesn't try to judge semantic equivalence for always-escalate fields, so a cosmetic-only edit still escalates
a single time becoming a range is a real logistics change (earlier setup/delivery window), and would escalate either way
a field with real content going blank is treated as a likely extraction miss, always escalated by rule ahead of every other check
same blank-field-regression rule as location, different field -- confirms it's field-agnostic
critical priority check: proves the blank-detection rule fires BEFORE the guest_count percent-change branch, not after -- a blank new_value should never reach _pct_change() at all

critical determinism check: event_type normally routes to the LLM judge, which would make this eval non-deterministic -- but the blank-detection rule short-circuits BEFORE that branch is ever reached, so this stays a pure rule decision with no API call
adversarial: an all-whitespace string isn't literally empty, but .strip() reduces it to '', so this still counts as a blank-field regression, not a real edit to '   '

adversarial edge case: old_value was ALREADY blank-ish, so bool(old_value.strip()) is False and the blank-regression rule correctly does NOT fire (there's no real content-to-blank regression here) -- but the decision still lands on escalate via the ordinary always-escalate-field rule for location, a different code path reaching the same outcome

same whitespace-counts-as-blank check as above, on guest_count specifically -- proves priority over the guest_count threshold branch, the most important one to prove given it's the field most likely to otherwise resolve to review

adversarial: the string "0" is non-empty (bool("0") is True), so this correctly does NOT trigger blank-detection -- it instead falls through to the ordinary guest_count percent-change rule, where a drop from 80 to 0 is a 100% decrease, well above threshold, and escalates for that reason instead
25% increase, above the SIGNIFICANT_QUANTITY_CHANGE threshold (15%)
5% increase, below the significant-change threshold -- still shown, just not urgent
adversarial boundary case: exactly 15% (15/100) -- the rule is a STRICT greater-than 0.15, so exactly-at-threshold does NOT escalate
one guest past the exact-15% boundary case above (16%) -- confirms the strict-greater-than behavior flips at the very next integer
14%, just under threshold
exactly 15% (30/200) at a different base count -- confirms the boundary behavior isn't an artifact of the specific numbers used in the other boundary case
15.5% at the same base as the case above -- one guest past the boundary
a 75% DECREASE -- confirms the percent-change math uses abs(), so a drop in headcount escalates exactly like a comparable increase, not just growth
10% decrease, under threshold
exactly 15% decrease -- same strict-boundary behavior as the increase cases, confirmed on the decrease side
16% decrease, one guest past the boundary

adversarial: old_value of 0 makes a percent-change mathematically undefined (division by zero) -- the code special-cases this to infinity/always-significant rather than crashing or silently treating it as 0% unchanged

adversarial: "12O" (letter O, not zero) fails float() parsing, so pct_change returns infinity and this escalates by the same fallback as the zero-baseline case. This exercises the decision layer's OWN defensive fallback for a garbled number -- in production, extract.py's output-validation guardrail would normally catch a non-numeric guest_count at extraction time before it ever reaches this diff, but a legacy or manually-edited stored record could still reach here, so the fallback still matters
adversarial: non-numeric OLD value (not just new) also fails parsing and falls back to escalate -- confirms the fallback isn't one-sided

adversarial: neither value parses as a number at all -- still resolves to escalate via the same can't-assess-magnitude fallback, which also happens to be the right call here since a placeholder becoming a real estimate is genuinely worth a look
a single-guest bump (2%) stays review even at a small base count
2% at a much larger base -- confirms it's percent-based, not a fixed guest-count delta
a 150% increase on a tiny base count -- confirms small absolute numbers can still trip the percent threshold hard
adversarial: decimal-formatted strings (as might come from a spreadsheet export) at exactly the 15% boundary -- confirms float() parses '60.00' correctly rather than choking on the decimal formatting
same decimal formatting, one guest past the boundary (16.7%)

adversarial: leading/trailing whitespace around the numbers -- confirms float() strips it correctly rather than failing to parse and falling back to a different (still-correct-here) escalate path for the wrong reason
any menu item added is escalated unconditionally, regardless of magnitude
any menu item removed is escalated unconditionally
parentheses/special characters in the name don't affect the unconditional add rule
adversarial: even a trivial, low-stakes-looking item still escalates unconditionally -- the rule doesn't try to judge an item's importance by its name
same as above, on removal -- a supply item disappearing still needs the kitchen to know

cases.recipe_name: Build-Your-Own Taco Bar with Carne Asada, Al Pastor, and Vegetarian Options
cases.why: an unusually long/complex recipe name doesn't change the unconditional add rule
a name starting with a digit doesn't affect matching or the decision
an allergen-safe item disappearing is exactly the kind of thing that must never be silently dropped -- covered by the same unconditional rule as any other removal
adversarial: accented/unicode characters in the recipe name shouldn't break matching or the decision rule
adversarial: even a blank/malformed recipe name (a plausible bad-extraction artifact) still escalates -- the ADD fact itself is what matters to this rule, not whether the name is readable
a quantity embedded in the name itself doesn't change the unconditional removal rule
a quantity/unit change on an existing item is a rule-decidable prep-volume fact, always escalated
adversarial: unlike guest_count, menu qty/unit changes have NO magnitude threshold at all -- a single-unit bump (10%) still escalates
a decrease escalates exactly like an increase -- no direction-dependence in this rule
same number, different unit (EACH vs LB is a real prep-volume-relevant change, not cosmetic) -- escalates
fractional quantity values don't affect the rule -- it doesn't parse magnitude at all for menu items
large-batch quantities still hit the same unconditional rule

adversarial: '33' and '33.00' are numerically identical -- this is a PURELY cosmetic reformatting, not a real quantity change, but the rule escalates it anyway. Documents a known false-positive-by-design tradeoff: contract_agent.py doesn't parse or compare the qty/unit magnitude for menu items at all, it escalates on the mere fact that the qty/unit STRING differs (see contract_store.diff_records, which is where this would normally be caught by whitespace/format normalization before ever reaching here -- this case tests the decision layer alone, bypassing that upstream step)
adversarial: same reasoning as the format-only case above, but for unit capitalization instead of numeric formatting -- still escalates despite being cosmetic
a zero-quantity item becoming real is a meaningful prep change, and escalates under the same unconditional rule
adversarial: a quantity dropped to zero (the item is effectively gone but still listed) is arguably close to a removal -- escalates either way under the unconditional qty/unit rule
